placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0078). This building does not stand centred on a lot at a typology setback: it stands ON the south face of blk_randolph_market, the block's Washington Street frontage, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is 1.50 m back from that lot line, which is the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and is not a measurement of this frontage, and its west wall is fixed by the west end of the run's own frontage, 1.5 m clear of the side lot line at that end. The bearing is the face's own, so the front looks square at Washington Street. The run carries no lateral offset, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the 1834 South Water Street view supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous working row of party walls rather than detached cottages set back on grass. The treatment is what this placement takes from it, and a run standing on any other face of the town is borrowing it from that one street: the view draws a row, it does not place this row. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot, and the side lot lines this row crosses were always conjectural.

THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Wright, Amasa” (tax_1833_113, line 165). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Wright' agrees with the entry's forenames; 6 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “A. Wright”. 2 lot rows, $1,040 in all: block 13 lot 15 at $480 (f1839_lot0238, printed page 49); block 13 lot 16 at $560 (f1839_lot0239, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 of those rows prints the bidder as a ditto mark under the name above rather than the name itself; 2 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Wright' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins A. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_lots_crosswalk_1835.json). frontage.why: T-0317, the successor T-0028's programme owes, and the first parcel in this project where the core density standard's corner clause and the end rule point in OPPOSITE directions. THE FACE IS MEASURED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, by the command T-A14 made of it — tools/measure_street_frontage.py randolph washington market franklin — and on the committed dataset Randolph carries 7 documented records and 7 inferred households against Washington's 1 and 0, Market's 2 and 1, and Franklin's 2 and 1. Randolph is this block's business face by the town's own record and it is FULL: the first deal took lots 0 and 2 and the inferred-household layer's two sawyer dwellings hold 4 and 6, so every lot on that face carries a roof and the two lots this block has left are both on the Washington tier. WHAT BINDS IS THE STANDARD'S THIRD CLAUSE. Lot 1 is the block's one free CORNER lot, the south-west one, fronting Washington along its long edge and Market Street along its short one, and a corner lot BUILDS TO THE CORNER — an east-anchored run packs back toward the middle of the face and stops wherever its roofs run out, so the corner is the one piece of frontage a row can never reach. The run is packed WEST to it. AND THE GRADING RUNS THE OTHER WAY, which is the finding here. On blk_randolph_dearborn's third deal the free corner was at Dearborn — the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835 — so building to the corner and standing the best roof nearest the crossing were the same act, and the parcel could not tell the two clauses apart. This corner is at MARKET, the far end of the face from that bridge, so they separate: the corner clause fixes WHERE THE ROW STANDS and the end rule fixes WHICH ROOF STANDS WHERE IN IT, and on this block they are demonstrably different questions. THE END RULE IS READ, NOT ASSERTED: tools/measure_end_rule.py reads this face at a spread of 71.03 m and a unit step of 6.07 m under the walked criterion and grades on it, while the same face under T-A11's straight line reads 4.82 m and is BELOW THE FLOOR — so the walk is what makes a grading possible here at all, and the straight line would have been grading this parcel's own declared setback invention. The row is therefore graded EAST, toward Franklin and the bridge beyond it: the meanest dwelling stands on the corner and the best closes the run at the east end. NO COORDINATE IS AUTHORED: the line, its bearing, the lot's own stretch of it and the end the run packs toward are all read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and the 1.5 m setback is the plat module's own lot margin rather than a measurement of this frontage. The Washington face carries no committed street wall for the run to adopt — the two roofs already standing on that tier are one-per-lot placements set back inside their own lots — so this run is the first line on the face and states the margin rather than adopting one.
